A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DataMIL work. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched across relocation and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original MetaWorld, LIBERO and real-robot OXE experiments, including benchmark comparisons, proxy-objective tests and qualitative analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds proxy comparisons, hyperparameter ablations, extended-training results and LIBERO selection analyses.

M1.justification: Both versions use clustered regression or metagradient datamodels, the behavior-cloning proxy, target-data splitting for OXE, ranked selection and downstream policy training. v2 provides operational details and pseudocode for the existing estimators; it does not establish a replacement algorithm, architecture or objective.

E1.justification: MetaWorld, LIBERO and the OXE subsets, robot embodiments and target tasks are retained. LIBERO-5 comprises five already evaluated LIBERO-10 tasks, and the extended proxy tests use tasks already covered by MetaWorld. These additions change analyses and experimental subsets rather than task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: Corresponding benchmark comparisons retain the same retrieval methods and Target-Only, All-Data or Random controls. New ablations reuse existing comparators. CUPID and COLLAGE enter the related-work discussion but are not evaluated as baselines; longer All-Data training changes its budget rather than its identity.

E3.justification: Appendix C introduces controlled evaluations varying selection percentages from 5% to 30%, clustering at 15 steps, 30 steps or whole trajectories, co-training ratios of 0.3/0.5/0.7, and All-Data training budgets of 1×/2×/4×. Main benchmark protocols are retained. Regression sampling is also reported as p=0.1 in v2 Appendix H, versus Bernoulli(1/2) in v1 Appendix B.2; this documentation change does not establish reruns.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands tests of the method's design choices: proxy-versus-rollout selection extends from one to four MetaWorld tasks, Figure 13 tests selection budget, clustering and co-training sensitivity, and Appendix C.6 checks whether longer training helps All-Data. Appendix A.2 adds LIBERO selection case studies. The no-goal MetaWorld analysis already existed in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report three MetaWorld seeds, five LIBERO seeds and one real-world seed. Figure 13 continues five-seed averaging. There is no new significance-testing or confidence-interval procedure; correction of an individual uncertainty value changes a result, not the reporting practice.

E6.justification: The LIBERO/OXE benchmark means in v1 Table 3 are retained in v2 Table 1, but v2 adds substantial sensitivity, proxy-comparison and qualitative results. Appendix C.6 reports All-Data success of 43.36, 44.13 and 38.40 at 1×, 2× and 4× training. The malformed STRAP Soup-Sauce uncertainty entry is also corrected to 15.7.

T1.justification: v2 Appendix B.3 adds explicit definitions of training-count perturbations and stochastic metagradient updates in Equations 11–12. Appendix B.2 generalizes inclusion probability from 1/2 to p. The underlying datamodel objective and first-order influence approximation were already present; moving the Taylor expansion into the main text is not new theory, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same central contributions: adapting datamodels to offline robotic data selection through a differentiable surrogate, scaling to larger policies and heterogeneous datasets, and improving task success. The additional evidence supports these existing claims without redefining their scientific scope.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations connecting reduced selection advantages at larger budgets to inclusion of more useful data, finer clusters to more precise selection, and excessive All-Data training to overfitting. It also interprets LIBERO retrieval through scene and object similarity. The computational, hyperparameter and target-scale limitations already existed in v1 and are consolidated into the conclusion.

D1.justification: Algorithms 1–2 and Appendices G–H substantially expand reproducibility information: estimator pseudocode, gradient averaging, 10,000 regression fits, sampling probability, MLP dimensions, metagradient iteration counts, training steps, the final 100-step differentiation window, optimizers and schedules. Hardware and runtime estimates are newly documented across the experimental settings.

R1.justification: v2 adds COLLAGE, CUPID, DataRater and work on scale transfer and robot dataset factors, while pruning several broad background references. It replaces v1's statement that robotic data attribution was unknown with a comparison to concurrent CUPID, emphasizing offline selection from heterogeneous datasets. The broader datamodel-versus-heuristic positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Targeted rewrites expand the metagradient explanation, tighten introductory and experimental prose, and improve appendix cross-references. The separate limitations section is merged into the conclusion, and existing appendix results are regrouped before implementation details. The overall narrative and most existing exposition remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with LIBERO selection plots, the extended proxy comparison, a three-panel ablation figure, two algorithm displays and a hyperparameter table. The real-world sample montage moves from v1 Figure 7 in the main text to v2 Figure 10 in the appendix. Existing benchmark tables and plots are largely retained.

improvement.justification: v1 left important estimator settings undocumented and several design choices weakly tested. v2's algorithms, hyperparameters and compute costs substantially improve reproducibility and feasibility assessment, while Appendix C tests surrogate validity, sensitivity and baseline training budgets. These address important evidential gaps without changing the main benchmark results. Some interpretation remains overstated: Figure 11 shows roughly a 20-point proxy deficit on dial-turn despite describing all deficits as small. This limits that conclusion but does not outweigh the substantial gains.
